moduleTitle: Redemption: the significance of the life, death, resurrection and ascension of Jesus for salvation and grace

note.specFocus: AQA 8062 Catholic Christianity, key beliefs: redemption – the significance of the life, death, resurrection and ascension of Jesus for Catholic beliefs about salvation and grace.
note.summary:
KEY IDEA: Redemption means "buying back" or rescuing. Catholics believe the whole Paschal Mystery of Jesus redeems humanity from sin and death and restores the relationship with God that was broken by sin. The Paschal Mystery is his life, passion, death, resurrection and ascension (CCC 571).

WHY REDEMPTION IS NEEDED: Genesis 3 describes the Fall. Adam and Eve disobey God, and sin and death enter the world. Catholics call the wounded human condition that results "original sin" (CCC 396–409). Humans cannot repair this relationship by their own efforts. "The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 6:23).

JESUS'S LIFE: His whole life is redemptive (CCC 517). Through his obedience to the Father, his teaching, healings and forgiveness of sinners, he shows God's love and restores what Adam's disobedience lost. Paul calls him the "new Adam" (1 Corinthians 15:22; Romans 5:19).

JESUS'S DEATH: Jesus freely gave his life "as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). His death on the cross is a sacrifice of atonement. He took the punishment that sin deserves and reconciled humanity with God ("at-one-ment"). "God so loved the world that he gave his only Son" (John 3:16). Catholics believe this sacrifice is made present, not repeated, at every Mass (CCC 1366–1367). The crucifix, which shows Christ's body on the cross, is a reminder of this.

RESURRECTION: On the third day Jesus rose bodily from the dead. The empty tomb is in Luke 24 and John 20, and the appearances to Mary Magdalene, the apostles and Thomas follow. The resurrection proves Jesus's victory over sin and death, confirms his divinity and is the guarantee of believers' own resurrection. "If Christ has not been raised, your faith has been in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:17). It is celebrated at the Easter Vigil, the high point of the Church's year, and every Sunday.

ASCENSION: Forty days after Easter, Jesus returned to the Father (Acts 1:6–11). He promised to send the Holy Spirit and to come again. The ascension shows that human nature has been taken into God's presence, so heaven is open to humanity (CCC 659–667). Jesus now intercedes for us, and the Church continues his mission.

SALVATION AND GRACE: Salvation is being saved from sin and its consequences and brought into eternal life with God. Grace is "favour, the free and undeserved help that God gives us" (CCC 1996). Catholics believe salvation is God's gift, received through faith and expressed in love and good works ("faith by itself, if it has no works, is dead", James 2:17). Grace comes especially through the sacraments: baptism removes original sin, reconciliation restores grace after serious sin, and the Eucharist nourishes it. Catholics also believe in the Church's role as the "universal sacrament of salvation" (Lumen Gentium 48).

DIFFERENT VIEWS: Many Protestants, following Luther, emphasise "justification by faith alone" (sola fide), though the 1999 Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification between the Catholic Church and Lutherans found broad agreement. Some liberal Christians see Jesus's death as a powerful example of self-giving love (moral influence) rather than a payment for sin. Some Christians understand the resurrection spiritually rather than physically.

KEY TERMS: redemption, atonement, sacrifice, original sin, Paschal Mystery, resurrection, ascension, salvation, grace, justification.

questions.question:
Which word means 'the free and undeserved gift of God's love and help'?
A) Atonement
B) Grace
C) Covenant
D) Repentance
questions.modelAnswer:
Answer: B) Grace.

The Catechism defines grace as 'favour, the free and undeserved help that God gives us' (CCC 1996). Atonement is reconciliation through Christ's sacrifice. A covenant is a binding agreement. Repentance is turning away from sin.
questions.examTip: Learn short definitions of the key terms: grace, atonement, redemption, salvation, sin.

questions.question:
Which event, described in Acts 1, happened forty days after the resurrection?
A) Pentecost
B) The Transfiguration
C) The Ascension
D) The Last Supper
questions.modelAnswer:
Answer: C) The Ascension.

Acts 1:3–11 describes Jesus appearing for forty days and then being 'lifted up' to heaven. Pentecost came ten days later (Acts 2). The Transfiguration and the Last Supper were before his death.
questions.examTip: Get the order right: Last Supper, crucifixion, resurrection, ascension (40 days), Pentecost (50 days).

questions.question: Give one reason why Catholics believe humans need redemption.
questions.modelAnswer:
Any one from:
• Because of original sin / the Fall of Adam and Eve (Genesis 3)
• Sin separates humans from God
• Humans cannot save themselves by their own efforts
• The 'wages of sin is death' (Romans 6:23)
questions.examTip: One clear reason only. 'Original sin' is a precise answer.

questions.question: Give one way in which Catholics believe they receive God's grace.
questions.modelAnswer:
Any one from:
• Through the sacraments (e.g. Baptism, the Eucharist, Reconciliation)
• Through prayer
• Through faith in Jesus Christ
• Through reading scripture / the Word of God
questions.examTip: 'The sacraments' or one named sacrament is the most precise answer.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which belief in the resurrection of Jesus influences Catholics today.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: Catholics celebrate the resurrection in worship (1 mark). Easter is the most important festival, centred on the Easter Vigil with the lighting of the Paschal candle. Every Sunday is a 'little Easter', which is why Catholics have a duty to attend Mass on Sundays (2nd mark).

Second way: The resurrection gives Catholics hope in the face of death (1 mark). Because Christ rose, they believe they too will be raised (1 Corinthians 15:20–22). Funerals are therefore times of hope, with the Paschal candle beside the coffin, and Catholics may face suffering and grief with trust in eternal life (2nd mark).
questions.examTip: Make the link clear: 'Because they believe Jesus rose… they…'.

questions.question: Explain two different Christian beliefs about how people are saved.
questions.modelAnswer:
First belief: The Catholic Church teaches that salvation is a free gift of God's grace, received through faith and expressed in good works and the sacraments (1 mark). Baptism begins the life of grace. Catholics are called to cooperate with grace by loving God and neighbour, since 'faith by itself, if it has no works, is dead' (James 2:17) (2nd mark).

Second belief: Many Protestant Christians, following Martin Luther, teach justification by faith alone (sola fide) (1 mark). They believe a person is put right with God simply by trusting in Christ's death, not by anything they do. Good works are the result of salvation, not a means to it, based on Ephesians 2:8–9: 'by grace you have been saved through faith… not the result of works' (2nd mark).
questions.examTip: Name the group holding each view (Catholic or Protestant) and give the scriptural reason behind it.

questions.question:
Explain two Catholic beliefs about the significance of Jesus's death.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First belief: Jesus's death is a sacrifice that atones for the sins of humanity (1 mark). Jesus freely offered his life in place of sinners, taking on the consequences of sin so that people could be forgiven and reconciled with God. That is why Catholics call him the Lamb of God (John 1:29) (2nd mark).

Second belief: Jesus's death shows the depth of God's love (1 mark). God was willing to give up his own Son rather than leave humanity lost. Catholics are called to respond with love and self-sacrifice of their own, 'taking up their cross' (Luke 9:23) (2nd mark).

Source of authority: Jesus says the Son of Man came 'to give his life a ransom for many' (Mark 10:45). This shows that he understood his death as freeing people from sin, in the way a ransom frees a captive. That is the meaning of redemption, 'buying back' (2 marks).
questions.examTip: Use the language of sacrifice, ransom and atonement accurately. These are specialist terms that earn credit.

questions.question:
Explain two Catholic beliefs about the ascension of Jesus.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First belief: The ascension marks Jesus's return to the Father in glory (1 mark). His mission on earth was complete. In his risen body he entered God's presence, and he now 'sits at the right hand of the Father', as the Nicene Creed says, reigning as Lord and interceding for humanity (2nd mark).

Second belief: The ascension opens heaven to humanity and begins the mission of the Church (1 mark). Because Jesus took his human nature into heaven, Catholics hope to follow him (CCC 661). Before ascending, he commanded the apostles to be his 'witnesses… to the ends of the earth', and he promised the Holy Spirit (2nd mark).

Source of authority: In Acts 1:9–11 Jesus is 'lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight'. Angels then say he 'will come in the same way'. This teaches that the ascension is not the end of the story: Christ will return at the Second Coming, so Catholics live in hope and readiness (2 marks).
questions.examTip: The ascension is often overlooked. Learn what it means (return to glory, heaven opened, mission and Spirit, Second Coming).

questions.question:
'The resurrection is more important than the crucifixion for Catholics.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• refer to Catholic teaching
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

St Paul says that 'if Christ has not been raised, your faith has been in vain' (1 Corinthians 15:17). Many people were crucified by the Romans. What makes Jesus unique, according to Christians, is that he rose from the dead. The resurrection proves he is the Son of God, shows God's approval of his sacrifice and reveals his victory over death.

The resurrection is also the source of Catholic hope. Because Christ rose, believers will be raised too (1 Corinthians 15:20–22). This is why Catholic funerals are hopeful, with the white pall and Paschal candle. The Church's calendar reflects the importance of the resurrection. Easter is the 'feast of feasts', and Sunday, the day of resurrection, is the Lord's Day on which Catholics must attend Mass.

ARGUMENTS AGAINST

Catholic teaching sees Jesus's death as the act of redemption itself. Jesus came 'to give his life a ransom for many' (Mark 10:45), and his sacrifice atones for the sin of the world. Without the crucifixion there would be no sacrifice, no forgiveness and nothing to rise from. The two events form one Paschal Mystery (CCC 571) and cannot be separated.

The crucifixion is at the centre of Catholic worship. The Mass makes present the one sacrifice of Calvary (CCC 1366). The crucifix, showing Christ's body, hangs in every Catholic church, whereas many Protestant churches use an empty cross. Catholics pray the Stations of the Cross and the Sorrowful Mysteries of the Rosary. They venerate the cross on Good Friday. This all suggests the crucifixion is at least as important as the resurrection.

The crucifixion also speaks powerfully to suffering people. It shows a God who shares human pain. Catholics are called to 'take up their cross' (Luke 9:23), and many find in Christ's suffering a meaning for their own.

CONCLUSION

There are strong reasons on both sides. The resurrection confirms Jesus's identity and gives hope, while the crucifixion is the sacrifice that brings redemption. The most convincing conclusion, and the one closest to Catholic teaching, is that neither is more important. They are two parts of one saving event. The cross without the resurrection would be a tragedy, and the resurrection without the cross would have no sacrifice for sin. That is why the Church celebrates them together in the Easter Triduum, from Good Friday to Easter Sunday.
questions.examTip: When two things are linked, it is a strong evaluative move to argue that they are inseparable. Do still give real arguments for each side first.

questions.question:
'Doing good works is the only way to be saved.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• refer to Catholic teaching
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

Jesus's parable of the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25:31–46) suggests that people are judged by what they have done. Feeding the hungry, welcoming strangers and visiting prisoners lead to eternal life, and failing to do these leads to punishment. 'Just as you did it to one of the least of these… you did it to me' (25:40). James 2:17 says that faith 'by itself, if it has no works, is dead'.

Some people argue that a good God would not exclude someone who lived a genuinely loving life simply because they did not belong to a particular faith. Many non-religious people believe goodness is what matters most, and that a just God (if one exists) would reward it.

ARGUMENTS AGAINST

Catholic teaching says salvation is first of all God's gift, not something we earn. Grace is 'free and undeserved' (CCC 1996). No one can save themselves from sin. Only Jesus's death and resurrection redeem humanity, and 'there is salvation in no one else' (Acts 4:12). Good works are important, but they are a response to grace and done with its help, not a way of buying our way into heaven. So 'the only way' is wrong.

The sacraments and faith are also part of the way to salvation. Jesus says, 'no one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and Spirit' (John 3:5), which Catholics apply to Baptism. Faith in Christ, repentance and the sacraments of Reconciliation and the Eucharist are means by which God's saving grace is received.

Protestant Christians go further. Following Luther and Ephesians 2:8–9 ('by grace you have been saved through faith… not the result of works'), they teach justification by faith alone. For them, works are the fruit of salvation, never its cause.

At the same time, the Catholic Church teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know Christ, but who seek God sincerely and try to do his will through conscience, 'may achieve eternal salvation' (Lumen Gentium 16). Even here, salvation comes through Christ's grace working in them.

CONCLUSION

Good works clearly matter. Matthew 25 and James show that faith without love is empty, and Catholics reject a faith that makes no difference to how one lives. But the claim that good works are the only way to be saved contradicts Catholic teaching that salvation is God's gift of grace through Christ. The more convincing view is that salvation comes through grace, received in faith and the sacraments and lived out in good works. Works are necessary as the response to grace, but they are not the only or the first thing.
questions.examTip: Watch for absolute words like 'only'. They often let you argue for a balanced 'both… and' conclusion.
